problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###  

**a. Verdict:**  
I have found a complete solution. The minimum possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Permutation reduction.**  
   By permuting the columns we may assume the uncovered squares are the diagonal cells \((i,i)\) for \(i=1,\dots ,n\) where \(n=2025\).

2. **Construction (upper bound).**  
   For each column \(j\) (\(2\le j\le n\)) place a vertical rectangle of size \((j-1)\times1\) covering the cells \((1,j),(2,j),\dots ,(j-1,j)\).  
   For each column \(j\) (\(1\le j\le n-1\)) place a vertical rectangle of size \((n-j)\times1\) covering the cells \((j+1,j),\dots ,(n,j)\).  
   These are \(2n-2\) disjoint rectangles that cover every cell except the diagonal.

3. **Lower‑bound set.**  
   Let  

   \[
   S=\{(i,i+1)\mid 1\le i\le n-1\}\cup\{(i,i-1)\mid 2\le i\le n\},
   \]

   the squares immediately to the right and to the left of each diagonal hole.  
   \(|S|=2n-2\).

4. **Key Lemma.**  
   *No axis‑parallel rectangle can contain two distinct squares of \(S\) without also containing a diagonal square \((k,k)\).*  
   Proof proceeds by case analysis of the possible pairs of squares in \(S\); in every case the minimal rectangle that contains the pair necessarily includes a diagonal cell.

5. **Consequences of the Lemma.**  
   Because each tile is a rectangle and must cover all squares of \(S\), each element of \(S\) must lie in a different tile. Hence any admissible tiling uses at least \(|S|=2n-2\) tiles.

6. **Conclusion.**  
   The construction shows that \(2n-2\) tiles are sufficient, and the lemma shows that fewer tiles are impossible. Therefore the minimum number of tiles equals \(2n-2\).  
   For \(n=2025\) this gives \(2\cdot2025-2=4048\).

---

### Detailed Solution ###  

Let  

\[
n=2025 .
\]

A placement of tiles is a family \(\mathcal T\) of axis‑parallel rectangles whose interiors are pairwise disjoint and whose union consists of all unit squares of the \(n\times n\) board except a set \(H\) of uncovered squares.  
The condition *“each row and each column has exactly one uncovered square”* means that  

\[
H=\{(i,p(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}
\]

for some permutation \(p\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\); each row \(i\) contains the uncovered square \((i,p(i))\) and each column \(j\) contains the uncovered square \((p^{-1}(j),j)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1. Reduction to the diagonal  

Permuting the columns of the board does not change the number of tiles needed: a rectangle \([r_1,r_2]\times[c_1,c_2]\) is transformed into \([r_1,r_2]\times[\sigma(c_1),\sigma(c_2)]\) where \(\sigma\) is the column permutation.  
Choose \(\sigma=p^{-1}\); after this column permutation the uncovered squares become  

\[
H'=\{(i,i)\mid 1\le i\le n\},
\]

the main diagonal.  
Consequently it suffices to solve the problem for the diagonal holes; the obtained minimum will be the same for any permutation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2. A tiling with \(2n-2\) tiles (upper bound)  

For each column \(j\) with \(2\le j\le n\) define  

\[
R_j^{\text{up}}=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le j-1\},
\]

a vertical rectangle of size \((j-1)\times1\).  
For each column \(j\) with \(1\le j\le n-1\) define  

\[
R_j^{\text{down}}=\{(i,j)\mid j+1\le i\le n\},
\]

a vertical rectangle of size \((n-j)\times1\).

Set  

\[
\mathcal T=\{R_j^{\text{up}}\mid 2\le j\le n\}\cup\{R_j^{\text{down}}\mid 1\le j\le n-1\}.
\]

The family \(\mathcal T\) contains \((n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) rectangles.  

*Coverage.*  
If a cell \((i,j)\) satisfies \(i<j\) it belongs to \(R_j^{\text{up}}\); if \(i>j\) it belongs to \(R_j^{\text{down}}\).  
The diagonal cells \((i,i)\) belong to none of the rectangles.  

*Disjointness.*  
For a fixed column \(j\) the two rectangles \(R_j^{\text{up}}\) and \(R_j^{\text{down}}\) are separated by the single row \(i=j\); they do not intersect.  
Different columns involve disjoint sets of cells, so all rectangles are pairwise disjoint.

Thus \(\mathcal T\) tiles the whole board except the diagonal, using exactly \(2n-2\) tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3. A lower bound of \(2n-2\) tiles  

Define  

\[
S=\bigl\{(i,i+1)\mid 1\le i\le n-1\bigr\}\cup
   \bigl\{(i,i-1)\mid 2\le i\le n\bigr\}.
\]

Geometrically, \(S\) consists of the squares immediately to the right of each diagonal hole (except the rightmost column) together with the squares immediately to the left of each diagonal hole (except the leftmost column).  
Clearly  

\[
|S|=(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2.
\]

---

**Lemma.** *No axis‑parallel rectangle can contain two distinct squares of \(S\) without also containing a diagonal square \((k,k)\).*

*Proof.*  
Consider two distinct squares of \(S\).

1. **Both from the right‑hand family:** \((i,i+1)\) and \((j,j+1)\) with \(i<j\).  
   The smallest rectangle containing them has row interval \([i,j]\) and column interval \([i+1,j+1]\).  
   Since \(i+1\) lies in both intervals, the cell \((i+1,i+1)\) (a diagonal hole) is inside the rectangle.

2. **Both from the left‑hand family:** \((i,i-1)\) and \((j,j-1)\) with \(i<j\).  
   The minimal rectangle has rows \([i,j]\) and columns \([i-1,j-1]\).  
   Because \(i\le j-1\), the cell \((i,i)\) (a diagonal hole) belongs to the rectangle.

3. **One from each family:** \((i,i+1)\) and \((j,j-1)\).  
   Assume \(i\le j\) (the opposite case is symmetric).  
   The rectangle’s rows are \([i,j]\) and its columns are \([i+1,j-1]\).  

   *If \(j\ge i+2\)*, then \(i+1\) lies in both intervals, so \((i+1,i+1)\) (a diagonal hole) is inside.  

   *If \(j=i+1\)*, the two squares are \((i,i+1)\) and \((i+1,i)\); the rectangle is the \(2\times2\) block with rows \(\{i,i+1\}\) and columns \(\{i,i+1\}\), which contains the diagonal holes \((i,i)\) and \((i+1,i+1)\).  

   Hence in every sub‑case a diagonal cell is included.

Thus any rectangle that contains two distinct elements of \(S\) must also contain a diagonal hole, which is forbidden for a tile. ∎

---

Because each tile is a rectangle and must cover all squares of the board except the diagonal, every element of \(S\) must lie in a distinct tile (otherwise a tile would contain two elements of \(S\) and consequently a diagonal hole). Consequently any admissible tiling uses at least \(|S|=2n-2\) tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4. Minimality  

Section 2 provides a tiling with exactly \(2n-2\) tiles, and Section 3 proves that no tiling can use fewer. Therefore the minimum possible number of tiles equals \(2n-2\).

For the original board with \(n=2025\),

\[
2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4050-2 = 4048 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5. Answer  

\[
\boxed{4048}
\]
